evidences.text: baesystemsai.blogspot.co.uk /2017/02/lazarus-watering-hole-attacks.html On 3rd February 2017, researchers at badcyber.com released an article that detailed a series of attacks directed at Polish financial institutions.
ANALYSIS As stated in the blog, the attacks are suspected of originating from the website of the Polish Financial Supervision Authority (knf.gov[.]pl), shown below:

The C&Cs given in the BadCyber analysis were the following IP addresses: 125.214.195.17 196.29.166.218 LAZARUS MALWARE Only one of the samples referenced by BadCyber is available in public malware repositories.
WATERING HOLE ANALYSIS The attacker content on the compromised sap.misapor[.]ch site was not accessible at the time of writing.
ADDITIONAL WATERING HOLES The eye-watch[.]in domain appears to have been used in watering-hole attacks on other financial sector websites.
A further instance of the malicious code appears to have been present on a bank website in Uruguay around 2016- 10-26 when a PCAP of browsing to the website was uploaded to VirusTotal.com.
ADDITIONAL MALWARE AND EXPLOIT ACTIVITY The compromised eye-watch[.]in domain has been associated with other malicious activity in recent months.
It is worth noting that these samples were all compiled after the domain began being used alongside the knf.gov[.]pl watering-hole.
The malware attempts to run a series of commands with cmd.exe and then returns the result via the C&C, eye-watch[.]in .
Host: www.eye-watch[.]in SILVERLIGHT XAP FILE 'cambio' is Spanish for 'change' .
The URL is similar to that noted in the BadCyber blog, and the use of an XAP file matches what can be found in the Archive.org cache for the sap.misapor[.]ch site.

Despite this potential connection to the Poland bank compromises, the malware is not particularly advanced – for example using basic operations to gather system information. The malware attempts to run a series of commands with cmd.exe and then returns the result via the C&C, eye-watch[.]in .

cmd.exe /c hostname cmd.exe /c whoami cmd.exe /c ver cmd.exe /c ipconfig -all cmd.exe /c ping www.google.com cmd.exe /c query user cmd.exe /c net user cmd.exe /c net view cmd.exe /c net view /domain cmd.exe /c reg query "HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Internet Settings" cmd.exe /c tasklist /svc cmd.exe /c netstat -ano | find "TCP"
AppManifest.xaml Shell_siver.dll System.Xml.Linq.dll

Together they form a re-packaged exploit for Silverlight based on CVE-2016-0034 (MS16-006) – a Silverlight Memory Corruption vulnerability. The exploit has previously been used by several exploit kits including RIG and Angler to deliver multiple crimeware tools.
The Shell_siver.dll file contains a compile path:
Once the payload stub is decoded, it represents itself as a PE-image, which is another .NET 4.0 assembly with the internal name binaryreader.dll .

This second-stage DLL assembly, binaryreader.dll , is heavily obfuscated. The DLL (MD5 hash: 7b4a8be258ecb191c4c519d7c486ed8a ) is identical to the one reported in a malware traffic analysis blog post from March 2016 where it was used to deliver Qbot. Thus it is likely the code comes from a criminal exploit kit which is being leveraged for delivery in this campaign.
